question: A clear and recurring pattern of problems with Turkish pepper imports into the EU, due to excessive or banned pesticides, has been recorded in 2025–2026. In 2025, the RASFF system recorded 27 European alerts for Turkish peppers, of which eight concerned the substance formetanate, a toxic substance not accepted even in Türkiye.

In 2026, the serious incidents continued: Bulgaria activated multiple alerts for peppers with abamectin and pirimiphos methyl, while in another case tebufenopyrad was detected at approximately 35 times above the EU limit, resulting in the classification of ‘serious risk’ and the import of the load being prohibited at the border.

At the same time, Romania issued a warning about Turkish red kapya peppers due to excess cadmium. These substances are linked to neurotoxicity, cholinesterase inhibition, possible effects on child development, liver toxicity and, in the case of cadmium, long-term carcinogenic effects.

Organisations such as PAN Europe and Greenpeace Türkiye are now speaking out about a systemic problem concerning the reliability of Turkish food exports. Unfortunately, the Greek authorities have not reported the detection of contaminated Turkish peppers over the past two years. At the same time, Greece exceeds the EU average in blood cancers, non-Hodgkin lymphomas, leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes.
In view of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the current framework for protecting consumers against imports of substances associated with serious haematological and neurotoxic effects to be adequate?
How does the Commission assess the adequacy of the checks carried out by the Greek authorities on imported Turkish fruit and vegetables with repeated RASFF notifications?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) To ensure compliance with EU food safety requirements, the Member States must carry out risk based official controls and enforcement activities in line with Regulation (EU) 2017/6251. Where food of non-animal origin from third countries poses a risk, the Commission may adopt measures through Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17932.

The results of official controls of consignments of Turkish peppers entering Greece does not raise concerns as regards detection of non-complaint consignments. The Commission performs audits in Member States to verify in particular the application of the substantive rules and of the control rules.

Ther Commission also performs audits in third countries to ensure that goods intended for export to the EU comply with the applicable EU rules and that the control system is capable of ensuring it3. An audit of the import control system in Greece is planned in late 2026 which will include the official controls on high-risk imported fruit and vegetables.

General monitoring of residues in the EU coordinated multiannual control programme is based on an assessment of European Food Safety Authority which identified 36 products but does not single out Greece or banned substances exclusively. Member States tailor their riskbased sampling programmes. The Commission established a Task Force4 to make import controls more efficient, which will focus e.g.
on pesticide residues and will consider coordinated EU action on specific imported products.
